fatal_errors: The proposed SPS treatment is unrelated to the target intervention: liquid-metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu.
The initial material is misidentified as an already formed, defective W–Cu composite rather than an as-cast WTaVTi alloy with sacrificial Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels.
The mechanism omits selective Ti–Cu exchange, retention of W/Ta/V-rich ligaments, formation of bicontinuous aligned Cu channels, and the approximately 300 nm W-rich passivating interlayer.
The proposed 1000–1100 °C, under-15-minute processing window conflicts with the reported 1200 °C, 96-hour liquid-metal-dealloying condition.
The cited evidence does not establish that short-cycle SPS heals W–Cu interfaces or improves their thermal conductivity and irradiation stability.
Irradiation stability of the treated composite is predicted without support; the target study irradiated precursor dendrites as a proxy, not the finished composite.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad fusion-joint motivation and proposes a controlled comparison with thermal and microscopy measurements, but it does not reconstruct the material, intervention, processing conditions, architecture, or mechanism of the target study. Its thermal-conductivity prediction is only generically directionally consistent. It also conflates irradiation stability with direct testing of a finished composite and supplies no irradiation species, energy, fluence, or relevant endpoint. The proposed falsification experiment could test the SPS idea, but it is not sufficiently specified and would not discriminate the target liquid-metal-dealloying mechanism. E1 concerns an Al-matrix composite, E2 concerns annealed and irradiated refractory alloys, and E3 discusses SPS behavior of another high-entropy material at about 2300 °C; none validates the claimed W–Cu SPS intervention.
